name: Portfolio Optimisation Beyond Mean and Variance
title: Portfolio Optimisation Beyond Mean and Variance
answer: Portfolio optimisation beyond mean and variance moves past the Markowitz framework that uses only expected return and volatility. It incorporates higher moments such as skewness and kurtosis, downside risk measures like conditional value at risk, and drawdown constraints. The approach is used where asset returns are non-normal, as is common among AI-related equities and instruments. It treats portfolio construction as a problem of shaping the full distribution of outcomes rather than trading off two summary statistics.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Portfolio optimisation beyond mean and variance moves past the Markowitz framework that uses only expected return and volatility. It incorporates higher moments such as skewness and kurtosis, downside risk measures like conditional value at risk, and drawdown constraints. The approach is used where asset returns are non-normal, as is common among AI-related equities and instruments. It treats portfolio construction as a problem of shaping the full distribution of outcomes rather than trading off two summary statistics.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on daily price histories, corporate filings, and structured event data. The site's dataset includes daily prices for 117 listed AI-related instruments, 353 merger and acquisition filings, and 432 company pages, which can serve as inputs for feature engineering and scenario generation. Optimisation models are typically implemented in numerical computing environments and solved with convex or non-convex solvers, depending on the risk measure chosen. Data pipelines must handle missing values, corporate actions, and asynchronous updates across sources.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners replace or augment the variance term with coherent risk measures such as expected shortfall, or with penalised objectives for tail loss and maximum drawdown. Scenario-based optimisation draws on historical stress periods and Monte Carlo simulation to capture dependence beyond linear correlation. Machine learning is used to estimate return distributions, regime probabilities, or covariance matrices that adapt to changing market conditions. Constraints on turnover, liquidity, and exposure to specific AI subsectors are layered onto the objective.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance and model risk are central because optimisation outputs depend on estimated inputs that can be unstable. The site tracks 142 active AI lawsuits and 210 compliance and regulation pages, which portfolio teams may use as inputs for risk overlays and scenario definitions. No optimisation model removes the need for human review of data quality, assumption changes, and the legal status of underlying instruments. Rights to use third-party data and the interpretability of model outputs are documented as part of the portfolio construction process.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward optimisation that learns from market structure and adapts to regime shifts without overfitting. Causal inference and reinforcement learning are being explored for dynamic rebalancing and transaction cost aware execution. Generative models may produce synthetic stress scenarios that fill gaps in historical data. Explainability and auditability are likely to become standard requirements as these methods move into production portfolio systems.
